transcript:
Fireflies.ai Meeting Transcript

Title: Technical deep dive: demo fallback routing + graceful degradation
Date: 2025-12-09
Time: 16:02 UTC (08:02 PT)
Duration: 56 minutes

Attendees
- Avery Johnson (Redwood Inference, AE)
- Simran Kaur (Redwood Inference, Enterprise demo architect)
- Mina Haddad (Redwood Inference, Fallback routing owner)
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference, Demo technical owner)
- Rita Chandra (Summit Telecom, Director Platform Engineering)
- Ben Wallace (Summit Telecom, Staff SRE)
- Elena Petrova (Summit Telecom, Security Architect)
- Tomás Alvarez (Summit Telecom, Procurement Ops)

Auto-Summary (generated)
- Summit wants deterministic routing (pinned model/version) but also wants “never fail closed” behavior under capacity events.
- Redwood explained routing layers: model pins, compatible fallback sets, region preferences, and tier-based degradation (quality vs cost vs latency).
- Discussed how to demo fallback safely (synthetic traffic + controlled capacity constraint) without implying output unpredictability.
- Security/residency: Summit needs strong controls around cross-region routing; Redwood can restrict fallbacks to region/zone or disable cross-region.

Topics
1) What triggers fallback (capacity, model health, latency SLO breach, 5xx)
2) Compatibility + “same family” fallbacks (quantized variants, context limits)
3) Demo story: graceful degradation vs “we changed your model”
4) Region / residency controls
5) Observability and auditability

Questions (captured)
- Can we guarantee no model change unless an explicit policy says so?
- Is fallback deterministic, or can it oscillate request-to-request?
- Can we pin to a model + minor version and still allow emergency patching?
- How do we prove to auditors that regulated traffic didn’t cross regions?

Transcript

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Cool, I think we’re recording. Thanks everyone for hopping on. Today is meant to be a technical deep dive specifically on fallback routing. So less “what is Redwood” and more like, how the routing policies work, what we can and can’t guarantee, and also how we’re planning to show this as part of the demo story without it feeling… spooky.

[00:19] Rita Chandra: Yeah, that’s exactly it. Our platform folks are worried that “fallback” equals “uncontrolled change.” And SRE worries it equals “surprise blast radius.”

[00:30] Avery Johnson: Makes sense. Simran and Mina are on—Mina owns the fallback routing stuff. Markus also owns the demo tenant, so he can talk about what we can show reliably.

[00:41] Simran Kaur: Hey all.

[00:43] Mina Haddad: Hi everyone.

[00:45] Ben Wallace: Hi. Also just to set context, we’ve been burned with managed endpoints where a model deprecates or the provider changes something and suddenly our p99 goes weird. So we’re trying to avoid that class of incident.

[01:02] Mina Haddad: Totally fair. Let me start with the mental model. There are basically three layers:
1) Route configuration (what a client hits: a stable name like “support-agent-prod”).
2) A “primary target” which is usually a pinned model version.
3) A fallback set which is explicit and constrained—by model family, quantization profile, max context, and optionally region.

[01:24] Elena Petrova: When you say “explicit,” do you mean you can’t fallback to something unless we list it?

[01:29] Mina Haddad: Correct. Default policy can be “no fallback.” For customers that want high availability, you can say “fallback allowed,” but it’s still constrained by a compatibility set. In the demo environment we set it up intentionally so it’s very controlled.

[01:44] Rita Chandra: And what are the triggers? Like, what makes it actually switch?

[01:50] Mina Haddad: Triggers are policy-driven. Common ones:
- Hard failure: model unavailable, 5xx, health check failing.
- Capacity: request would exceed quota or we can’t admit it under the SLO.
- Latency guardrail: if primary is breaching p95 or p99 for a window, you can route a fraction or all.
- Region availability: if a region is degraded and you permit cross-region.

[02:18] Ben Wallace: The capacity one worries me. That can flap.

[02:21] Mina Haddad: Yep, if you do it naïvely. We add hysteresis and minimum dwell times. Also you can do “canary” routing: route 1% to fallback first, check error rate/latency, then increase.

[02:36] Simran Kaur: And for demo specifically, we usually show a deterministic version: we simulate a primary failure, and you see the route fail over. It’s not “maybe it happens,” it’s “watch this switch.”

[02:47] Markus Klein: Yeah, because in a live demo, flappy behavior is the worst. We prefer the scripted “known-good” scenario.

[02:55] Rita Chandra: Okay. So talk to me about “pinned model version.” Is it pinned to, like, a major/minor? Or an exact artifact hash?

[03:06] Mina Haddad: In most cases, exact version ID. Internally it maps to a specific build. The route can say “model = Redwood-Llama-70B, version = 2025-11-17.2” (example). And you can specify allowed patch updates if you want emergency security or bugfixes.

[03:26] Ben Wallace: That’s like “stay on this but allow .x patch”?

[03:29] Mina Haddad: Exactly. But it’s opt-in. If you do strict pin, it stays strict.

[03:36] Elena Petrova: For regulated, we’d want strict. And we’d want no cross-region fallback. Even cross-AZ we can discuss, but cross-region is a no.

[03:46] Mina Haddad: Understood. We can set “fallback_regions = [eu-central-1]” (just as an example) and disable “global” fallback. Also we can ensure logs show the region and target selection.

[04:01] Simran Kaur: There’s also a demo angle here: “graceful degradation” doesn’t have to mean cross-region. It can mean: in the same region, you fallback to a smaller compatible model or a quantized variant.

[04:14] Rita Chandra: But that’s still a model change.

[04:17] Simran Kaur: It is, yes. The point is you control it. It’s better than returning 500s. And you can choose what “degradation” means: maybe lower quality, maybe lower max tokens, maybe disable tool calls. It’s policy.

[04:32] Avery Johnson: And to be clear, we don’t want to position it as “we change your model whenever.” It’s “you define a safety net.”

[04:41] Ben Wallace: So what about “oscillation” in a bad time? Like, some requests hit primary and some hit fallback and then our evals get noisy.

[04:52] Mina Haddad: Good question. Two options:
- Sticky routing: hash-based stickiness by conversation/session ID.
- Batch-level stability: once a route is in fallback mode, it stays for N minutes before re-evaluating.

[05:09] Ben Wallace: Sticky by conversation ID would be important.

[05:13] Mina Haddad: Yep. Also if you do tool calling workflows, you usually want the same model for the whole tool loop. So we recommend stickiness by “request_group_id” for the workflow.

[05:27] Elena Petrova: How do you audit it? Like, can we prove “this request went to model X in region Y?”

[05:34] Mina Haddad: We emit route decision logs. In Console you can see the route, the selected target, reason code (primary_ok, primary_unavailable, capacity_protect, latency_protect), and region. For enterprise, you can export that to your SIEM.

[05:52] Markus Klein: For demo, we show a simplified view—like a rollout / routing view that shows “primary” and “fallback” and the traffic split.

[06:01] Rita Chandra: Is that the Console view you showed in the last demo? The one with the little bars.

[06:05] Markus Klein: Yeah. Sometimes transcription calls it “rollout view” or “route rollout.” Same thing.

[06:10] Ben Wallace: Another question—compatibility. You said “same family.” How do you define that? Because context window differences matter.

[06:20] Mina Haddad: Compatibility rules include:
- Model architecture/family (e.g., Llama-3.1 style vs something else)
- Max context length (don’t route a 64k request to an 8k model)
- Tool calling support / structured output mode
- Quantization profile constraints (int8 vs fp16, etc.)

[06:39] Ben Wallace: And KV cache behavior? We rely on long conversations.

[06:43] Mina Haddad: Right—KV cache is per target. If you route mid-conversation to a different target you can’t reuse that KV cache. That’s why stickiness is recommended. And in practice, “fallback mid-conversation” is usually not what you want. More like, new conversations start on fallback during an incident.

[07:03] Rita Chandra: So the story is: the route flips state, but it’s not bouncing per turn.

[07:08] Mina Haddad: Exactly.

[07:11] Simran Kaur: And for the “graceful degradation” demo, we usually frame it as: “When capacity gets tight, Redwood can keep your app up by applying the policy you defined. Here’s what it looks like operationally, and here’s the audit trail.”

[07:28] Avery Johnson: Rita, can I ask—what’s your priority? Is it more “never fail” or more “never change outputs?”

[07:36] Rita Chandra: For regulated workflows, never change, even if it means erroring. For non-regulated, keep it up.

[07:44] Avery Johnson: That’s a clean split.

[07:46] Elena Petrova: Yep. We can categorize traffic by project or route.

[07:50] Mina Haddad: That’s how we’d implement it. Separate routes with separate policies. Route A: strict pin, no fallback, same region only. Route B: pinned + fallback within region to a smaller model. Route C: allow cross-region if permitted (maybe not for you).

[08:10] Ben Wallace: What about “dedicated capacity” in this context? Because with dedicated, fallback is less needed, right?

[08:17] Mina Haddad: It’s less needed for capacity, but still useful for “model health” or “bad deploy.” Like, if a new version is causing errors, you can rollback or temporarily route to previous. The same primitives apply.

[08:30] Markus Klein: Also demo-wise, we talk about Dedicated as “predictable throughput + isolation,” then fallback as “resilience.”

[08:39] Rita Chandra: Okay. But show me what the policy looks like. Like an example.

[08:45] Mina Haddad: I’ll describe it. It’s something like:
- primary: model=“rw-llama-70b”, version=“2025-11-17.2”, region=“eu-west”
- fallback_targets: [“rw-llama-70b-quant”, “rw-llama-8b”]
- constraints: same_region=true, max_context>=16k
- triggers: primary_unhealthy OR admission_control
- stickiness: session_id
- dwell_time: 10m

[09:16] Ben Wallace: Admission control meaning you’re rejecting to protect SLO.

[09:20] Mina Haddad: Right. Instead of just timing out, we can route to a target that can meet the SLO.

[09:27] Ben Wallace: That’s good. But we’d want transparency—like, we don’t want to silently degrade and then customer support says “the model got dumb.”

[09:36] Simran Kaur: Yes, and that’s part of the story. You can set a header or response metadata that indicates “fallback_used=true” so your app can show a banner or log it.

[09:49] Elena Petrova: Does that metadata leak sensitive stuff?

[09:52] Mina Haddad: It’s configurable. It can just be a boolean and a reason code. No payload.

[09:58] Rita Chandra: That would help. Because then we can correlate incidents.

[10:02] Avery Johnson: Also, on the demo side, we’d show it visually, not as a scary “trust us.”

[10:10] Markus Klein: Yeah. And we can also show the “reason code” in the trace view. Sometimes it’s “capacity_protect” or “primary_5xx.”

[10:21] Ben Wallace: Are you doing this at the request router layer or at the engine layer?

[10:27] Mina Haddad: Router layer (control plane / data plane router). The engine exposes health metrics; router uses that plus policy. The engine doesn’t randomly pick.

[10:39] Ben Wallace: Good.

[10:41] Rita Chandra: What about when a model is rolling out a new version. We’ve seen providers do like “silent refresh.”

[10:48] Mina Haddad: We don’t do silent refresh on pinned routes. If you opt into “floating” you can get automatic updates, but demos and most enterprise routes do strict pins.

[11:01] Simran Kaur: In our demo tenant we pin explicitly to avoid surprises when the model catalog changes.

[11:08] Ben Wallace: If you allow patch updates, how do you keep it from regressing quality?

[11:15] Mina Haddad: That’s where evals come in. You can gate a rollout on a prompt set + evaluation. So the flow is: version candidate -> canary traffic -> eval gate -> promote. If it fails, route stays on old version.

[11:33] Rita Chandra: That’s interesting. But I’m not sure we’d trust a vendor’s eval.

[11:38] Avery Johnson: You can bring your own prompt set and metrics. The tooling is in Console.

[11:44] Markus Klein: And for the demo, we seed a prompt set and show the “pass/fail” gate, but it’s synthetic.

[11:53] Elena Petrova: Synthetic is good. We don’t want any real data in the demo.

[11:58] Simran Kaur: Yes—our demo tenant is all synthetic traffic and synthetic logs.

[12:05] Ben Wallace: Back to fallback: how fast does it switch? Seconds? Minutes?

[12:11] Mina Haddad: For hard failure, seconds. For latency-based triggers, it depends on your window—like 30s to 2m. We don’t want to flap on one slow request.

[12:24] Ben Wallace: Makes sense.

[12:26] Rita Chandra: How do you test this? Because we’d want to simulate “primary is unhealthy” without actually breaking prod.

[12:35] Mina Haddad: We support a “fault injection” mode in non-prod environments. For prod, you can do controlled canary: artificially reduce capacity to the primary target or temporarily mark it as “drain.”

[12:49] Markus Klein: In the demo we do the “drain” approach so it’s safe.

[12:54] Ben Wallace: Drain like in Kubernetes? You take it out of rotation.

[12:58] Mina Haddad: Similar concept. We call it “deprioritize” or “drain.”

[13:05] Simran Kaur: The graceful degradation demo beat is: we show a route, then we “drain” the primary and watch traffic shift to fallback, then we restore it.

[13:16] Rita Chandra: Okay, but what’s the messaging? Because “we degrade quality” is not a great selling point.

[13:23] Avery Johnson: We usually phrase it as “keep user-facing flows up.” Like, your app can still answer basic questions even if the premium model is constrained.

[13:33] Simran Kaur: And we clarify: you choose the fallback targets. Some customers choose “same model, different quantization” so quality change is minimal, but cost/latency changes.

[13:44] Ben Wallace: Quantization… people always say it’s the same but it’s not always.

[13:49] Mina Haddad: True. That’s why we treat it as a different target and you can test it with your evals.

[13:56] Elena Petrova: Residency again—if fallback is in-region, fine. But if you do cross-region, what about logs, traces, etc.

[14:04] Mina Haddad: We can keep logs in-region as well, depending on the deployment mode. For Private/VPC deployments, you control where telemetry goes.

[14:14] Elena Petrova: That’s more for the Private offering.

[14:17] Avery Johnson: Right. But even in hosted, we can scope routing and data to regions where we have support.

[14:25] Rita Chandra: We’re likely Private or at least VPC. Hosted is tough for us.

[14:30] Simran Kaur: Understood. In the meantime, the demo tenant is hosted, but we can speak to Private architecture with diagrams and screenshots.

[14:41] Ben Wallace: Okay. Another scenario: partial outage. Suppose the model is up, but streaming disconnects. Then what?

[14:49] Mina Haddad: Streaming is treated like a transport capability. If streaming failures cross a threshold, policy can route to a target/region where streaming is healthy, if allowed. Or you can fallback to non-streaming mode with shorter max tokens.

[15:07] Ben Wallace: Hmm. That’s interesting. But again, could cause changes in user experience.

[15:11] Mina Haddad: Yes. The point is you can make an explicit choice: “I’d rather return non-streaming than fail.”

[15:18] Rita Chandra: For us that might be okay for some apps.

[15:22] Avery Johnson: Ben, what are your SLOs? Like p95 and p99 targets.

[15:27] Ben Wallace: For interactive, p95 under 1.5 seconds to first token, p99 under 3 seconds. For batch, we care throughput and cost.

[15:38] Mina Haddad: Great. So a policy could specifically look at TTFT (time to first token) and error rate, not just overall latency.

[15:47] Markus Klein: In Console we display TTFT and per-token latency breakdown. Sometimes the transcription calls it “time to first taken.”

[15:56] Ben Wallace: (laughs) Yeah.

[16:00] Rita Chandra: What about cost controls? If you fallback to a smaller model, cost changes. If you fallback to same model in another region, cost changes.

[16:09] Mina Haddad: You can set a “cost ceiling” preference as well. But generally fallback is about availability. For cost, we recommend proactive routing rules like: use smaller model for low-risk routes, larger for high-value.

[16:24] Simran Kaur: That’s another demo module, but we can keep today to reliability.

[16:30] Avery Johnson: Yep.

[16:32] Elena Petrova: If we do Private, do we still get the same routing capabilities?

[16:38] Mina Haddad: Yes, same policy engine. Control plane might be deployed in your VPC. Some features like global routing obviously depend on your topology, but the primitives are the same.

[16:53] Rita Chandra: Okay. Now tell me about “graceful degradation” more concretely. Like what do you suggest we show to our execs that doesn’t feel like a science project.

[17:04] Simran Kaur: Exec-friendly version is:
1) Show normal operation: pinned model, stable performance.
2) Introduce a failure mode: “capacity spike” or “primary unhealthy.”
3) Show that the app continues to answer and the platform shows “fallback in effect.”
4) Show audit trail and easy rollback.

[17:27] Markus Klein: And we keep a backup screenshot/recording in case the live environment has issues.

[17:33] Ben Wallace: Is the fallback selection deterministic in the set? Like if you list two fallbacks, which one is used?

[17:41] Mina Haddad: You can specify ordering and weights. Default is ordered list: try first fallback, if it’s not admissible, then second.

[17:52] Ben Wallace: Great.

[17:54] Elena Petrova: And can you guarantee “no cross-tenant contamination” in demo? Sorry, I know that’s not today, but we’ve seen demo environments where logs leak.

[18:03] Markus Klein: Demo tenant is isolated. Separate org, separate projects, synthetic traffic. We also scope API keys and rotate them. No customer data in it.

[18:12] Elena Petrova: Good.

[18:14] Rita Chandra: Let’s talk about “model family” again. If your primary is like Llama 70B, and fallback is Llama 8B, behavior differences are big.

[18:25] Mina Haddad: Yes, and that’s why some customers choose “same size, different quantization” as fallback. Or same size, different deployment pool. Like dedicated pool A vs pool B.

[18:39] Ben Wallace: That’s the better story for us. Keep semantics stable.

[18:44] Simran Kaur: We can do that in the narrative. “Fallback doesn’t have to mean smaller; it can mean same model on a different capacity tier.”

[18:55] Avery Johnson: Which ties into Dedicated.

[18:57] Rita Chandra: Okay. But then, capacity. If the same model is constrained, is the fallback really available?

[19:05] Mina Haddad: If it’s in a separate pool, yes. That’s the point of isolation. Also, fallback can be regionally redundant if you choose.

[19:15] Ben Wallace: But we won’t choose cross-region for regulated.

[19:18] Mina Haddad: Right. Then we’d focus on separate pools within region.

[19:24] Rita Chandra: So what exactly do we need to configure to do “separate pools within region”? Is that Dedicated or can Hosted do it?

[19:33] Avery Johnson: Hosted can do tiers, but Dedicated is the cleanest story: reserved capacity, predictable throughput, and you can still have a backup pool.

[19:45] Ben Wallace: That’s more of a commercial conversation.

[19:48] Avery Johnson: Yep, we can keep it technical today.

[19:51] Simran Kaur: For the demo, we can still show the controls in a “Dedicated-style” way even if the demo tenant isn’t literally your dedicated pool. We’ll be clear it’s illustrative.

[20:05] Rita Chandra: Okay.

[20:07] (crosstalk)

[20:08] Ben Wallace: Observability: do you emit metrics we can scrape? Or is it all in Console.

[20:13] Mina Haddad: Both. There’s Console dashboards, and we have export for metrics (Prom-compatible in Private, and webhook/export options in hosted). For fallbacks, we emit counters: fallback_used_total, reason_code, route_id, target_id.

[20:33] Ben Wallace: Great.

[20:35] Elena Petrova: Audit logs—are routing policy changes audited?

[20:39] Mina Haddad: Yes. Route config changes are in audit logs with actor, timestamp, diff summary.

[20:47] Elena Petrova: And SSO/RBAC is supported. Just checking.

[20:51] Avery Johnson: Yes. For enterprise.

[20:53] Markus Klein: In the demo we can show the audit log view, but we have a “safe sharing” version, no sensitive info.

[21:01] Rita Chandra: Good.

[21:03] Ben Wallace: How do you avoid the “fallback hides underlying problem” issue? Like, we want to know primary is bad.

[21:10] Mina Haddad: We alert on fallback usage. If fallback rate crosses a threshold, you get an alert. Also you can set “fallback max percentage” so it can’t silently become the new normal.

[21:25] Ben Wallace: Nice.

[21:27] Simran Kaur: That’s another strong demo point: “Resilience with guardrails.”

[21:33] Rita Chandra: Okay I like that phrasing.

[21:36] Avery Johnson: (laughs) Noted.

[21:38] Rita Chandra: One more: If a request is too large for fallback (context too big), what happens?

[21:46] Mina Haddad: Policy can say “do not fallback if incompatible.” Then you either error or you can have a special “truncate” behavior. But truncation is risky. Most enterprise customers prefer explicit error.

[22:02] Ben Wallace: Explicit error.

[22:03] Elena Petrova: Explicit error.

[22:05] Simran Kaur: Yep.

[22:07] Avery Johnson: Cool.

[22:10] Tomás Alvarez: Sorry, I joined late—Tomás. I’m mostly here for procurement timing later, but just listening.

[22:16] Avery Johnson: Hey Tomás.

[22:18] Rita Chandra: We’re deep in routing policy land.

[22:21] Tomás Alvarez: Yeah sounds… fun.

[22:25] Ben Wallace: (laughs)

[22:27] Avery Johnson: Rita, Ben—would it be useful if Mina sent a short written doc with the routing knobs? Because I know this is a lot.

[22:36] Rita Chandra: Yes, please. Preferably with examples for “regulated strict” and “non-regulated resilient.”

[22:43] Mina Haddad: I can send that.

[22:45] Ben Wallace: And include the “stickiness” part.

[22:48] Mina Haddad: Yep.

[22:50] Elena Petrova: And region restriction.

[22:52] Mina Haddad: Yep.

[22:54] Simran Kaur: I can also propose the exact demo segment so it aligns with that split. Like “Route A strict, Route B resilient.”

[23:04] Rita Chandra: Great.

[23:06] Ben Wallace: Before we close, can you talk about how you prevent “fallback to worse security posture.” Like, different region might have different controls.

[23:15] Mina Haddad: That’s why region allowlists exist. Also, fallback targets are not just “any model,” they’re targets you pre-approve. So you can ensure the fallback is in the same compliance boundary.

[23:29] Elena Petrova: Good.

[23:31] Ben Wallace: Okay. And what about “vendor-managed updates” to the fallback model? Like, if fallback is floating.

[23:39] Mina Haddad: Same rules. If you pin fallback targets too, then no changes. If you allow floating fallback, then you should gate it with evals. But we recommend pinning for enterprise.

[23:54] Rita Chandra: Okay.

[23:56] (pause)

[24:00] Avery Johnson: Anything else on your list today?

[24:03] Rita Chandra: I think we hit the main concerns. The key is: “fallback is explicit and auditable.” And we can separate regulated vs non.

[24:13] Ben Wallace: Yeah. If you send docs, we’ll review and probably have follow-ups about how it integrates with our incident management.

[24:22] Avery Johnson: Perfect.

[24:24] Simran Kaur: We can also schedule a follow-up with your network folks to talk about Private/VPC routing and egress.

[24:32] Elena Petrova: Yes, we’ll want that.

[24:35] Avery Johnson: Great. Let’s do recap and next steps.

[24:39] Avery Johnson: Mina will send routing policy doc + config examples by Friday. Simran will send proposed demo script for graceful degradation that’s “safe” and doesn’t imply uncontrolled model changes. Ben will send SLO targets and any hard constraints, and Elena will confirm the data residency boundaries, specifically whether metadata/logs can be outside region. And we’ll schedule a Private/VPC networking follow-up.

[25:05] Rita Chandra: Sounds good.

[25:07] Ben Wallace: Works.

[25:08] Elena Petrova: Yep.

[25:10] Tomás Alvarez: And I’ll just note for later we may need SLA language around region constraints, but not for today.

[25:18] Avery Johnson: Noted. Thanks everyone.

[25:22] Meeting ended (recording continued briefly)

[25:25] (side chatter)

[25:27] Markus Klein: Simran, I’ll sync with you on the demo tenant flow—make sure the “drain primary” step is stable.

[25:33] Simran Kaur: Yep, and we need a backup screenshot if Console is flaky.

[25:37] Mina Haddad: I’ll include “dwell time” and “stickiness” examples in the doc.

[25:42] Recording stopped.
